title: How to select your first marketing channel: where customers are plus what comes naturally
summary: Jason Cohen argues your first marketing channel should sit at the intersection of where your customers already are and what you are naturally good at or genuinely want to master. Go deep on one channel, even a small one, and expand later from strength. If the overlap is empty, change the business or partner with someone for whom that channel is a superpower.

principles.text: Pick your first channel at the intersection of where customers already are and what comes naturally to you.
principles.quote: you should operate at the intersection of where the customers already are, and what comes to you naturally and joyfully.

principles.text: You can't control where customers hang out. Fish where the fish are.
principles.quote: You don't control where your customers already go for industry news or to discover new software. You have to fish where the fish are.

principles.text: Forcing an unnatural channel fails: audiences spot impostors, algorithms bury them, and your disdain leaks into the work.
principles.quote: Doing something unnatural, that you despise, will fail.

principles.text: A small channel where you can be a top creator beats being a tiny fish on a huge one, since algorithms promote the biggest voices.
principles.quote: It is better to be one of the top three creators on this topic on Threads than to be the 200th biggest creator on LinkedIn, even though LinkedIn has many more people.

principles.text: Win one channel first, then expand to adjacent ones from a position of strength, repurposing content and funding help with revenue.
principles.quote: Now you're expanding into a second marketing channel from a position of strength.

principles.text: If no channel fits both constraints, rethink the business or partner with someone who is a wizard at that channel.
principles.quote: Another possibility is you need to partner with someone for whom this particular marketing channel is their superpower.
